title: We are patchwork
hook: we are all patchwork, and each piece plays its own game (Essays 2.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, laughing and weeping. Your line was laugh, don't weep. Did you catch yourself being very important about something small, and smile? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-five.

Calm in the meeting, furious in the parking lot. Patient with a stranger's toddler, short with your own mother. Generous on Monday, petty by Thursday. So which one is the real you? Montaigne takes up that question in the essay that opens the second book of the Essays, and his answer is uncomfortable and oddly freeing. It's all of them, every one. And none of them stays in charge for long.
screen: `CALM HERE, FURIOUS THERE.` → `WHICH ONE IS REAL?` → `ALL OF THEM.`

segments.voice: First, the puzzle. In Of the Inconstancy of Our Actions, Montaigne says that people who study human behavior find nothing harder than fitting our actions together into one steady picture. We contradict ourselves so often that it's easier to believe we're changeable than consistent. So, he says, it's unfair to judge a person by a single act. Second, the image. We are all patchwork, he writes, so shapeless and mixed in our making that each piece, each moment, plays its own game. And then the line that stings: there's as much difference between us and ourselves as between us and other people. Third, the confession. He doesn't exempt himself. He says he turns his soul one way and shows one face, then turns it and shows another. He lists what he finds in himself: bashful and bold, talkative and silent, truthful and lying, generous and stingy. All of it, he says, depending on which side he looks from. Fourth, the week's patches. This week ends here, so look back. Imagination, which can make us ill or well. Custom, which makes anything seem normal. A head well made, not full. Who are the barbarians? The back shop. Laugh, don't weep. Montaigne never sews these into one system, and he doesn't try. Each essay is a patch. On an ordinary Tuesday, this one is a mercy, in two directions: toward the person who snapped at you, and toward the you who snapped back.
screen: `HARD TO BE CONSISTENT.` · `EACH PIECE PLAYS ITS OWN GAME.` · `BOLD AND BASHFUL, BOTH.` · `A WEEK OF PATCHES.` · then, large: `PATCHWORK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice two different yous. Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring back one moment from the last day or two when you were at your best: steady, kind, clear. Now bring back another when you were somebody else: rushed, sharp, small. Don't choose which one is real. Set them side by side, like two squares of cloth. Both are yours. Breathe with both of them there. Later today, watch for a third one showing up. The bell holds the time.
We are patchwork. Montaigne's picture of a person: made of pieces, each moment playing its own game, as different from ourselves as from others. Today's word.
Your line: patchwork. Today, before you sum someone up from one moment, including yourself, remember the other pieces. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-five.

screen: `DAY 1155 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE FALL FROM THE HORSE.`

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often take this essay as a reason to go slow in judging anyone, themselves included, by a single act.

original.script: chaque pièce, chaque moment, fait son jeu

original.note: French, from Of the Inconstancy of Our Actions: each piece, each moment, plays its own game.

trapdoor: what you thought: patchwork means being inconsistent, and that's a flaw to fix.
what it means: a person is many pieces and moments, so one act is a poor summary of anyone.
what a scholar hears: the essay opens Book Two, and Montaigne lists his own contradictions in it; he describes the patchwork from the inside and makes no attempt to sew it into one system.
